newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile fails to find radiation from Russian probe.
newsitem.headline: Chile fails to find radiation from Russian probe.

text.p: Chile's air force has not found any traces of radiation from the ill-fated Russian Mars 96 space probe that may have crashed into the Pacific Ocean close to Chile's north coast, said newspaper La Epoca on Saturday.

The paper, quoting air force officials, said a Hercules C-130 plane equipped with radiation monitors flew over the Chilean mainland and the Pacific to test for radioactivity and look for signs of wreckage.

The search followed a report from the U.S. space agency NASA that part of the probe, which was carrying eight ounces (200 grams) of plutonium, could have fallen in an area centred 20 nautical miles from the northern fishing port of Iquique.
Earlier reports said the satellite plunged into the ocean hundreds of miles (kilometres) farther east between the remote Easter Island and the Chilean mainland.

Although most of the probe was thought to be destroyed on re-entry, U.S. scientists said it was probable the rocket's four batteries containing the radioactive plutonium have fallen to the ocean floor.

Three Chilean naval ships are sailing to the area and will take samples of water to test for radioactivity, although it seems unlikely they will find any traces of contamination, said naval officials.
Russian experts have said that the batteries, each about the size of a roll of film, should be safe as they were designed to withstand the heat and stress on landing on Mars.
Environmentalists have said that any radioactive contamination could devastate the rich fishing grounds in the southern Pacific which attract trawlers from around the world.
The doomed Mars 96 probe crashed into the Pacific Ocean nearly two weeks ago after a booster rocket misfired, preventing it from breaking out of the Earth's gravity.
